passage:
In the HR room on the fourth floor, Yogesh kept his voice level, though his jaw was tight. Two weeks earlier the company had thrown a party for record profits. Yesterday his division was told it was being cut.

Dhruv, the HR partner, slid a form across the table. "I know this feels unfair."

"It does," Yogesh said. He had drafted a screaming email last night and never sent it. "I have questions instead. What is my notice period, in writing? How is severance calculated, and who signs off? What happens to my leave balance? And can you tell me which policy or clause governs all of this?"

Dhruv wrote each question down. "I can answer three now. I'll get the rest by tomorrow."

Yogesh nodded. The anger hadn't gone anywhere, but it was pointing at something useful now.

qa.q: What did Yogesh not do with the email he drafted the night before?
qa.a: Yogesh never sent the screaming email he had drafted.

qa.q: What is Yogesh feeling at the meeting, and how do we know?
qa.a: Yogesh is angry, shown by his tight jaw and the screaming draft, but he keeps his voice level and asks precise questions.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh choose questions instead of a public tirade?
qa.a: Precise questions about notice, severance and policy get him written answers and protect his future options, while a public outburst could shrink them.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see the meeting from the HR side?
qa.a: Dhruv may find it hard to deliver the news, and probably finds Yogesh's clear questions easier to answer than a shouted complaint.

grounding: Yogesh's rage at leadership after profit celebrations is channelled into precise questions about severance, notice and rights.

passage: Vikas, you're angry about the cuts. Good. I was too. When I was twenty-five, I was a young woman in the accounts team of a shipping company in Kochi. In March they threw a huge party for our record year, with a band on the lawn. In May, they cut thirty jobs, mine included. I shook with rage. I went home and wrote a letter to the newspaper calling the directors thieves. My father read it and said, "Sleep first." Next morning I tore it up. Instead I wrote down three questions: how much notice would we get, what compensation was due, and whether the union could check it. I asked them in the meeting, slowly, one by one. The HR man had to answer in writing. My old boss later gave me a reference, because I'd stayed sharp but fair. Anger is fuel, Vikas. Your Shalini-ammachi burnt it for the right engine.

qa.q: When was the party for the record year?
qa.a: In March, with a band on the lawn.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel when the cuts came after the party?
qa.a: Shalini felt furious and betrayed, shaking with rage.

qa.q: What turning point in the story channelled Shalini's anger usefully?
qa.a: After sleeping on it, she tore up the angry letter and asked precise questions on notice, compensation and union checks in the meeting.

qa.q: How might Shalini's father have seen the letter to the newspaper?
qa.a: He probably understood her anger but worried the public letter would harm her future, which is why he told her to sleep first.

grounding: An elder recalls rage at cuts after a record celebration, and channelling it into precise questions on notice and rights instead of a public tirade.

passage:
The all-hands video call kept freezing on Pranav's laptop because the café's internet was terrible, but he caught enough: forty jobs gone, including his. Six weeks ago the CEO had thrown a rooftop party to celebrate "our best quarter ever".
His face went hot. He opened the company social page and began typing a furious comment about champagne and pink slips. Gopika, laid off too, sat across from him. "Don't," she said. "Everyone who might hire you can read that."
He deleted it, fingers still trembling. Then he opened the call's question box and typed slowly while the video buffered:
"1. What is the notice period? 2. What severance is offered, and on what basis? 3. Where can we read our rights under our contracts? 4. Who in HR will answer these by Friday?"
He hit send. The frozen CEO stared back. Gopika copied his questions for her own list.

qa.q: What did the CEO celebrate six weeks earlier?
qa.a: "Our best quarter ever," with a rooftop party.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling as he began typing the comment?
qa.a: He felt furious and betrayed, his face hot, because the cuts came right after a lavish celebration.

qa.q: How did Pranav channel his anger usefully?
qa.a: He deleted the public comment and asked precise written questions on notice, severance, contract rights and an HR contact by Friday.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Pranav's first reaction?
qa.a: Gopika understands the anger, being laid off too, but is worried a public outburst would hurt both their future chances.

grounding: Rage at leadership after a record celebration is channelled into precise questions on severance, notice and rights instead of a public tirade.
